title: Many true readings (12.31)
hook: one screenshot, two opposite readings: Augustine says one verse can bear more than one true meaning, held in charity
tomorrow: why does the seventh day in Genesis never get an evening?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a bishop admitted he couldn't define time, then found it in the mind: memory, attention, expectation. The line was if no one asks.

One screenshot gets passed around a friend group, and two people read it in opposite ways. Both have reasons. Both are smart. And the chat gets tense anyway, because each is sure the other missed the point. Augustine knew that room. In book twelve of the Confessions he spends pages on one verse: "In the beginning God created heaven, and earth." And on the readers who disagreed with him about it. So, does one of them have to be wrong?
screen: `ONE SCREENSHOT, TWO READINGS.` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `DOES ONE HAVE TO BE WRONG?`

segments.voice: Two views live inside the Church on this, and both have a real case. The first says a text means what its author meant. Pin that down, and you're safe; let it go, and a verse can be bent into anything. Augustine takes that seriously. He wants to know what Moses meant. The second view is Augustine's surprise. He lists several readings of that first verse, and says more than one can be true. Then he turns to the readers who insist their reading is the only one Moses could have meant. He suspects they love it because it's theirs, not because it's true. Truth, he says, isn't my private property or yours; it belongs to everyone who loves it. And his test for any reading: is it true, and does it fit love of God and neighbor? That's where today's line comes from. Argue, yes, but in charity. The Catechism holds both views together. It says every sense of scripture rests on the literal sense, what the human authors meant. And it names spiritual senses built on that, so one passage can teach about Christ, about how to live, and about where life is headed.
screen: `VIEW ONE: WHAT THE AUTHOR MEANT.` · `VIEW TWO: MORE THAN ONE TRUE READING.` · `TRUTH BELONGS TO ALL WHO LOVE IT.` · `THE CATECHISM HOLDS BOTH.` · then, large: `IN CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who reads something that matters differently than you do: a verse, a family rule, a decision. Say their reading out loud, quietly, in its strongest form, as if you had to defend it. Then let it sit beside yours without answering it.
Many true readings. Augustine's claim that one verse can bear more than one true meaning, as long as it's true and charity holds.
Your line: in charity. Truth belongs to everyone who loves it, including the one across the table. Go gently.

howItsDone: Catholics read scripture with the Church, attending first to the literal sense and then to the spiritual senses the Catechism names; Bible study groups often hear more than one faithful reading of a passage.

fork.setup: your study group reads Jonah. one friend says it's about God's mercy even for enemies; another says it's about running from your calling. both fit the text. what would Augustine do?
options: grant both can be true, test each against love, and keep arguing in charity.
work out which one the author meant, and drop the other as wrong.

fork.reveal: in book twelve Augustine grants more than one true reading of a verse, but not just any: it has to be true, and the argument has to keep charity.

original.note: Latin: charity, love. Augustine's rule for arguing over what scripture means.

chat.says: dad and abuela read ruth at dinner. dad: go where you're called. abuela: stay with family. who's right?
options: Maybe both. Augustine says one verse can hold more than one true reading, held in charity.
Abuela. The oldest reading is what the author meant, so dad's has to be wrong.
Neither. A verse means whatever you need it to mean that day, so pick yours.
chat.meaning: Ruth leaves her homeland and also refuses to leave Naomi. Augustine grants more than one true reading, if it's true and fits love.

Augustine.meaning: the North African bishop who wrote the Confessions

Moses.meaning: tradition's author of Genesis, as Augustine read it

literal sense.meaning: what the human authors of scripture meant

spiritual senses.meaning: further meanings the Catechism says rest on the literal sense

Catechism.meaning: the Catholic Church's summary of its teaching
